Abstract
The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) and edge computing technologies has expanded the attack surface 
for cybercriminals, emphasizing the need for robust and efficient cybersecurity measures. Intrusion detection 
systems (IDS) are essential defenses; however, deploying traditional IDS solutions on edge devices remains 
challenging due to limited computational, memory, and energy resources. This research proposes an energy-
efficient IDS framework based on a modified Deep Neural Network with Knowledge Distillation and Quantization 
(DNN-KDQ) to address these challenges. The CICIDS2017 dataset was preprocessed to extract energy-centric 
features, and adaptive sampling and model compression techniques were applied to optimize performance. The 
proposed DNN-KDQ model achieves a prediction test accuracy of 99.43%, reduces model size from 196.77 KB to 
20.18 KB, and achieves an inference time of 0.07 ms per sample in real-time scenarios. These results demonstrate 
the feasibility of deploying high-accuracy, low-latency IDS models on resource-constrained edge devices, 
contributing to more scalable and energy-efficient cybersecurity solutions for modern network infrastructures.

Introduction
Context
The digitization process provides numerous benefits 
to the energy sector, including improved forecasting, 
predictive maintenance, demand-side opportunities, 
enhanced system operation, and more efficient measure­
ment and monitoring systems [1]. Additionally, digital 
transformation has contributed to mitigating cybersecu­
rity challenges [2]. However, the energy industry remains 
highly vulnerable to cyber threats such as supply chain 
attacks, ransomware, and data breaches. The increas­
ing reliance on digital technologies and widespread data 
usage necessitates strict adherence to privacy, security, 
safety, and ethical standards, particularly concerning 
cybersecurity threats [2].
The scalability and operational efficiency of energy 
systems have significantly improved with advancements 
in digitalization, including smart grids [1, 3] renew­
able energy networks [4], and Internet of Things (IoT)-
based energy management devices [2, 5]. Despite these 
improvements, digital transformation introduces new 
cybersecurity risks. Cyberattacks targeting these infra­
structures, such as Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), 
unauthorized access, and data manipulation, can cause 
operational disruptions, financial losses, and security 
breaches [6]. Strong cybersecurity measures, includ­
ing network segmentation, intrusion detection systems 
(IDS), and regular security audits, can help mitigate these 
risks [7]. Furthermore, employee awareness and training 
programs are crucial for recognizing common attack vec­
tors and identifying suspicious activities.
IDS play a vital role in protecting energy infrastruc­
tures by monitoring network traffic and detecting poten­
tial security threats. These systems generate alerts upon 
detecting unauthorized access or suspicious activity. IDS 
solutions can be categorized into three main types: signa­
ture-based, anomaly-based, and hybrid IDSs. A primary 
challenge for signature-based IDS is the need for con­
tinuous updates to detect emerging threats effectively [8]. 
Traditional IDS techniques, such as rule-based and sig­
nature-based methods, have shown effectiveness against 
known threats [9]. However, deploying deep learning 
(DL)-based IDS solutions in energy systems presents 
challenges, including high computational requirements, 
energy inefficiency, and latency concerns. These issues 
are critical in real-time and resource-constrained opera­
tional environments.
Traditional IDS models, while effective in central­
ized or high-performance computing environments, 
encounter significant challenges when deployed in 
edge environments. Specifically, these models typically 
demand substantial computational power, large memory 
footprints, and persistent network connectivity, all of 
which are constrained in edge devices. Edge computing 
environments often involve battery-powered or low-
resource devices that prioritize energy efficiency, making 
heavyweight IDS models impractical. Moreover, tradi­
tional IDS solutions are not optimized for real-time pro­
cessing under tight latency constraints, which is critical 
for timely threat detection at the edge. The large model 
sizes and complex feature extraction processes also strain 
local storage and processing capabilities, resulting in 
increased inference delays and reduced system respon­
siveness. These limitations necessitate the development 
of lightweight, energy-efficient IDS models capable 
of maintaining high detection accuracy with minimal 
resource consumption, as addressed in this research.
This research tackles these challenges by develop­
ing a DL-based, energy-efficient IDS for modern energy 
infrastructures. The primary goal is to enhance security 
without compromising efficiency by designing IDS mod­
els optimized for low power consumption and real-time 
responsiveness. However, DL models often require a 
large number of parameters, making them computation­
ally expensive. While advancements in hardware, such as 
high-performance GPUs, TPUs, and cloud computing, 
have facilitated DL adoption, edge devices still face limi­
tations in storage capacity and model inference speed. 
Researchers have explored lightweight DL techniques, 
such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and filter 
pruning, to address these constraints [10, 11].
Weight compression techniques aim to reduce the 
memory requirements of model parameters, often lever­
aging efficient encoding strategies to minimize storage 
and memory access demands. Quantization simplifies 
computational processes, reduces model size, and opti­
mizes bit-width for local computations on IoT devices. 
By replacing complex 32-bit floating-point calculations 
with lower-bit multiplications, inference acceleration is 
achieved. Low-precision quantization techniques trans­
form full-precision weights and activations into 8-bit 
integer values using integer-arithmetic inference frame­
works, while maintaining bias parameters at 32-bit to 
preserve baseline accuracy [12].
Various intrusion detection techniques and analytical 
models are available for securing energy systems. DL, 
a subset of machine learning, leverages multi-layered 
artificial neural networks to learn hierarchical data rep­
resentations. Its ability to generate feature hierarchies 
from large-scale unlabeled data makes it well-suited for 
analyzing complex, high-dimensional datasets [13]. Many 
IDS solutions incorporate DL models, achieving high 
detection performance. Figure 1 provides an overview of 
the real-time DL-Based IDS Approach.

Objective
With the increasing interconnectivity of energy systems, 
they have become more susceptible to cyberattacks. One 
of the critical challenges in these systems is the need for 
real-time threat detection, yet existing IDS often experi­
ence delays due to high computational demands. Many 
energy systems, particularly edge and IoT devices, have 
limited energy and processing capabilities, making them 
unsuitable for complex IDS solutions. While DL can 
enhance intrusion detection, its high resource require­
ments pose significant constraints. The primary objec­
tive is to design an IDS that achieves an optimal balance 
between energy efficiency, detection accuracy, and real-
time performance. To address these challenges, this 
research introduces the DNN-KDQ model, which lever­
ages DL and energy optimization techniques to enhance 
security in energy systems.

edge devices, demonstrating high performance with

Literature review
Current research
IDS play a crucial role in securing IoT networks against 
cyber threats. Various approaches have been proposed to 
enhance the performance, accuracy, and efficiency of IDS 
solutions. This section reviews and discusses the diverse 
literature on ML-based IDS, highlighting their strengths 
and limitations.
Olanrewaju-George and Pranggono [14] developed 
an IDS leveraging federated learning to enhance anom­
aly detection and data privacy in IoT devices. Both 
supervised and unsupervised DL models were trained, 
demonstrating improved performance compared to 
non-federated learning methods. However, the approach 
lacks an evaluation of anomaly patterns across different 
devices, limiting its generalizability.
Prazeres et al. [15] proposed a distributed IDS archi­
tecture utilizing flow-based anomaly detection opti­
mized for resource consumption in IoT environments. 
The approach employed deep neural networks to detect 
malicious traffic and demonstrated a strong performance 
with 0.2 false positives and 0.1 false negatives. However, 
challenges remain in feature selection for anomaly detec­
tion due to device variability.
Poornima et al. [16] introduced a hybrid LDA-LR-
based IDS for edge computing, achieving an accuracy 
of 96.56% and a precision of 95.78%. The approach effi­
ciently detected various attack types but lacked scal­
ability analysis concerning the increasing number of IoT 
devices. Additionally, privacy issues in IoT data transfer 
remain an open research challenge.
Adabi et al. [17] integrated an IDS with a Security 
Information and Event Management (SIEM) system to 
provide real-time cyberattack detection. The system 
effectively identified DoS attacks, but high CPU and 
RAM usage in Elasticsearch indicated the need for opti­
mization to reduce resource consumption.
Qing et al. [18] introduced a robust multi-stage pro­
gressive autoencoder for anomaly detection in hyper­
spectral images. This approach demonstrated superior 
detection capabilities compared to state-of-the-art meth­
ods. However, anomalies remain challenging to detect 
due to low occurrence probabilities, and feature extrac­
tion techniques require further improvements for better 
detection accuracy.
Shahid et al. [19] proposed an optimized IDS for Indus­
trial IoT (IIoT) networks using Deep Transfer Learning 
(DTL) and bootstrap aggregation ensemble techniques. 
The model achieved 100% accuracy across 14 cyberat­
tack classes. However, the study did not address real-time 
intrusion detection challenges and lacked extensive test­
ing on diverse IIoT environments.

Research gap
Despite significant advances in the development of 
machine learning and deep learning-based IDS for 
IoT environments, several critical challenges remain 
unresolved.
First, many existing IDS models suffer from high com­
putational complexity and energy consumption, which 
makes them unsuitable for deployment on resource-con­
strained edge devices. Although some studies have pro­
posed lightweight frameworks, few have systematically 
optimized both computational overhead and energy effi­
ciency while maintaining high detection accuracy, par­
ticularly under real-time constraints.
Second, while model compression techniques such 
as knowledge distillation and quantization have been 
explored extensively in other domains (e.g., natural lan­
guage processing, computer vision), their application 
in IDS for IoT and edge environments remains limited. 
Few studies have integrated these compression strategies 
specifically to balance energy efficiency, detection perfor­
mance, and inference speed in intrusion detection tasks.
Third, most IDS solutions have not been rigorously 
adapted for scalable, real-time operation across dynamic 
network conditions, especially when considering diverse 
attack patterns and varying traffic loads. Real-time adapt­
ability, energy-aware sampling, and edge deployment 
strategies are often underexplored in traditional IDS 
research.
The proposed DNN-KDQ model directly addresses 
these research gaps by introducing an energy-optimized 
deep learning framework that combines knowledge 
distillation, post-training quantization, and adaptive sam­
pling for efficient, real-time intrusion detection on edge 
devices. This holistic approach not only reduces model 
size and inference latency but also enhances detection 
robustness across varying network conditions, paving the 
way for practical and scalable deployment in modern IoT 
ecosystems.
Methodology
This study aims to develop a DL-based secure IDS that 
ensures reliable and energy-efficient cybersecurity for 
contemporary network infrastructures. Figure  2, repre­
sents the framework of our proposed methodology.
Dataset selection and preprocessing
Selecting minimal but relevant features reduces compu­
tation and energy usage during model training and infer­
ence. In our research, the CICIDS2017 dataset is utilized 
for training and evaluation. It includes a comprehensive 
range of benign and attack traffic, including:
 	•
DOS attacks (GoldenEye, Hulk, SlowHTTPTest).
 	•
Brute Force attacks (FTP-Patator, SSH-Patator).
 	•
Web Attacks (Brute Force, SQL Injection).
A well-known benchmark for IDS, the CICIDS2017 
dataset was selected because it provides a comprehen­
sive representation of various attack methods and realis­
tic network circumstances. Based on the energy-centric 
approach, we used a few key features, such as traffic-
flow-based features, packet-based features, time-based

The selection of the CICIDS2017 dataset is particularly 
well-suited for energy-efficient IDS research because 
it offers a comprehensive and realistic representation 
of modern network traffic while providing a rich set of 
features critical for selective feature extraction. Unlike 
older datasets such as KDD99 or DARPA98, which lack 
traffic diversity and realistic payloads [30], CICIDS2017 
includes up-to-date benign and attack flows captured

After selecting the important energy-centric feature we 
used data cleaning techniques and Non-numeric fields 
i.e. Flow ID, Src IP, Dst IP, Timestamp, etc. were removed. 
Categorical fields like Protocol were encoded using label 
encoding to make them suitable for machine learning 
models. Additionally, we employed data normalization 
to guarantee consistent feature scaling. The Standard­
Scaler was utilized to normalize all numerical features, 
converting the data into a standard normal distribution. 
Stratified sampling [31] was then used to preserve the 
proportion of attack classes by splitting the dataset into 
80% training and 20% testing data. We analyze the impor­
tant features using correlation and feature importance 
analysis techniques [32]. For correlation analysis, Heat­
maps were used to visualize feature correlations, identify­
ing redundancies and highly correlated features. Figures 
3 and 4 represents the importance of feature correlation. 
On the base of important feature correlation, our model 
selects the parameter for real-time IDS detection.
A Random Forest model was employed to assess and 
rank the significance of each feature. To enhance intru­
sion detection accuracy while addressing dimensionality 
challenges, feature selection techniques were integrated 
into the Random Forest (RF) approach. This method 
allows devices to collaborate on intrusion detection while 
maintaining data privacy by preventing the disclosure of 
sensitive information [33]. Figure 5 illustrates the key fea­
tures of our dataset, which were classified using Random 
Forest techniques.
Model development
By identifying patterns in the network traffic, the DL 
models can classify an action as either normal or abnor­
mal. To evaluate the effectiveness of DL approaches, we 
developed and tested different DL models i.e.
Deep neural network (DNN) model
A robust security model is essential for an effective IDS 
system to enhance network protection. Reducing the 
number of layers in the Deep Neural Network (DNN) 
model helps minimize detection time delays and false 
positives while strengthening defense against cyber 
threats [34, 35]. The proposed detection strategies are 
tailored for large-scale networks while ensuring a stream­
lined design to avoid unnecessary complexity. The input

layer of the sequential model incorporates fully con­

To mitigate overfitting, dropout layers are strategically 
placed after the hidden layers, utilizing the “ReLU” acti­

by the “Adam” optimizer, configured with a learning rate 
of 0.001 and sparse categorical cross-entropy loss. The 
final output layer classifies intrusion types using a soft­
max function, ensuring precise detection and categoriza­
tion of threats.
Convolutional neural network (CNN)
CNNs have long demonstrated their effectiveness in 
the field of IDS. However, as cyber threats become 
increasingly sophisticated, the demand for more 
advanced detection methods continues to rise. CNNs 
excel at capturing spatial correlations within data, 
making them well-suited for hierarchical feature 
extraction [38]. The CNN model leverages convolu­
tional layers with a kernel size of 3 × 3, max pooling 
layers to reduce feature dimensions, and fully con­
nected layers for classification, effectively transform­
ing input features into 2D matrices. By employing 
these techniques, CNN architectures enhance their 
discriminative capacity, reducing noise and focusing 
on critical information, ultimately improving the accu­
racy and reliability of IDS detection [39].
Recurrent neural network (RNN)
The RNN model is specifically designed for sequen­
tial data analysis. It employs Long Short-Term Mem­
ory (LSTM) layers to capture temporal dependencies 
between network packets, enhancing intrusion detec­
tion accuracy [40]. Attack-related features are system­
atically categorized using the RNN, allowing for effective 
classification of different types of threats. At each level, 
the RNN processes incoming inputs while incorporat­
ing information from previous computations, ensuring a 
more comprehensive and context-aware analysis of net­
work activity [41].

Hybrid CNN-LSTM
The hybrid CNN-LSTM model effectively mitigates 
overfitting and computational complexity while ensur­
ing enhanced scalability by leveraging CNNs for effi­
cient feature extraction and LSTM networks for 
capturing temporal patterns [42]. Beyond improving 
detection accuracy, this model addresses the limita­
tions of conventional IDS techniques, providing a 
more adaptive and robust solution for modern network 
security challenges. The CNN-LSTM hybrid model 
integrates LSTM layers for sequential data learning 
and CNN layers for extracting essential features from 
the input data, resulting in a highly efficient and pre­
cise intrusion detection system.
Proposed DNN-KDQ model
In this research paper, we propose a modified DNN 
model that integrates energy optimization tech­
niques. We evaluate and compare different deep learn­
ing models, including DNN, CNN, RNN, and hybrid 
CNN-LSTM architectures, based on their effectiveness

Model compression techniques
To reduce model size and computational requirements, 
we apply two complementary compression techniques: 
quantization and knowledge distillation [44].
Real-time and edge computing applications face chal­
lenges due to parameter complexity. A widely used tech­
nique to address this issue is knowledge distillation (KD), 
a compression method designed for edge deployment. 
It generates a lightweight student model from a well-
trained teacher model, which is often released on public 
platforms [45, 46].
In our research, we employ offline knowledge distilla­
tion, where a larger teacher model (such as DNN, CNN, 
RNN, and hybrid architectures) is first trained, and its 
knowledge is subsequently transferred to a smaller stu­
dent model through a separate training process [47]. The 
student model minimizes a combined loss function that 
incorporates both the true labels and the softened out­
puts of the teacher model, ensuring high detection accu­
racy while reducing the number of parameters.
After knowledge distillation, we apply post-training 
quantization to further compress the student model. 
In this step, the model weights and activations are con­
verted from 32-bit floating-point representations to 8-bit 
integers. Quantization significantly reduces the model’s 
memory footprint and enables faster inference by allow­
ing efficient integer operations on CPUs and low-power 
edge devices, without requiring model retraining.
It should be noted that pruning techniques, which 
eliminate redundant weights or neurons, were not 
employed in this study to avoid compromising the detec­
tion accuracy of the proposed IDS model. Our focus was 
on maintaining a strong balance between compression 
and classification performance.

Edge deployment
In our research, Edge-AI leverages DNN-KDQ algo­
rithms that are directly integrated into devices, enabling 
local AI-based predictions while minimizing reliance on 
distant servers or cloud computing. This advancement 
facilitates the efficient execution of compact DNN-KDQ

This study highlights the significant impact of an 
embedded DNN-KDQ model on battery life and real-
time threat detection, achieving over 99% classification 
accuracy. The framework is validated through deploy­
ment on a Raspberry Pi 4. Optimization techniques 
include model quantization, reducing weight precision 
from 32-bit to 8-bit integers, enhancing computational 
efficiency.
The IDS is implemented on edge devices to minimize 
latency and distribute computational workloads. To fur­
ther enhance performance, hardware accelerators such 
as NVIDIA Jetson and Raspberry Pi are utilized for high-
efficiency, low-power deployment [50]. Additionally, to 
optimize energy consumption and integrate IDS into a 
scalable distributed framework, fog and edge computing 
architectures are employed.
Edge deployment strategies contribute to energy sav­
ings by enabling local data processing on edge devices 
instead of relying on continuous transmission to remote 
cloud servers. This reduces the energy expenditure 
associated with wireless communication and central­
ized infrastructure usage. Furthermore, local inference 
using lightweight, quantized models minimizes compu­
tational overhead and extends the operational lifetime 
of battery-powered devices, making the system highly 
efficient for real-time applications in energy-constrained 
environments.
Real-Time data integration
In real-time integration, continuous monitoring of net­
work traffic from energy systems and IoT devices is 
essential for detecting anomalies [51]. Sliding window 
techniques are employed to facilitate real-time anom­
aly detection, dynamically adjusting the window based 
on T-test and F1-based approaches. The F1 approach 
ensures a consistent upward trend in the F1 score, while 
the T-test detects time-series patterns and modifies the 
window accordingly [52].
As intelligent power systems become more prevalent, 
power devices exhibit increasing variability in size, shape, 
and specifications. To address this complexity, a sliding 
window-based data correction technique has been devel­
oped to handle low-dimensional missing data and high-
dimensional feature noise [53]. Additionally, an adaptive 
feature fusion method leveraging dictionary learning 
and feature dimension reduction is proposed to enhance 
model accuracy in detecting anomalous data [54].
To optimize efficiency, adaptive sampling is employed 
to ensure that the IDS processes only the necessary 
amount of network traffic, thereby conserving energy and 
improving overall system performance.
Alerting and mitigation
An effective alert system is essential for notifying opera­
tors of detected intrusions in real time. Alerting provides 
administrators with critical data, enabling them to pro­
actively or reactively manage and optimize network ser­
vices [55]. A comprehensive monitoring strategy should 
include automated mitigation mechanisms to minimize 
security risks. These strategies may involve isolating 
compromised nodes, rerouting traffic, or implement­
ing adaptive security policies to contain and neutralize 
threats efficiently.
System scalability
To enhance scalability across large energy networks, 
the DNN-KDQ model IDS architecture is designed 
for deployment using edge and fog computing. This 
approach ensures efficient data processing while reduc­
ing latency and network congestion. The lightweight 
DNN-KDQ edge device architecture is optimized for 
IoT environments, ensuring seamless compatibility with 
resource-constrained edge devices while maintaining 
high detection accuracy and energy efficiency.

presses the model by converting floating-point opera­

Conclusion
Recapitulation
This research introduces a low-power deep learning (DL) 
framework designed for real-time intrusion detection 
on edge devices. By integrating energy-efficient opti­
mization techniques with lightweight neural network 
architectures, the framework delivers high detection 
accuracy with minimal latency and power consumption. 
The proposed DNN-KDQ model, which leverages deep 
learning with energy optimization, demonstrated supe­
rior performance on the CICIDS 2017 dataset, achieving 
a balance between accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.
A comparative analysis of multiple deep learning 
models, including Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Con­
volutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural 
Networks (RNN), and hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures, 
confirmed that the DNN model, with its energy-efficient 
modifications, provided the best trade-off between detec­
tion accuracy and computational efficiency. This opti­
mization makes the model particularly well-suited for 
deployment in energy-critical infrastructures.
To further enhance efficiency, we applied energy com­
pression techniques, adaptive sampling, and advanced 
model quantization, reducing computational overhead 
while preserving detection accuracy. The framework also 
incorporates real-time anomaly detection, alerting mech­
anisms, and automated mitigation strategies, ensuring 
a comprehensive security solution for modern network 
environments. Additionally, its integration with edge and 
fog computing enhances scalability and minimizes reli­
ance on centralized computing resources, making it an 
effective solution for resource-constrained environments.
Despite these advancements, challenges such as adapt­
ing to evolving attack patterns and ensuring data privacy 
remain key areas for improvement. Addressing these 
limitations through continuous learning, federated learn­
ing, and improved regularization techniques will further 
enhance the framework’s resilience and applicability.
Future directions
Several avenues for future research can be explored to 
improve the proposed DNN-KDQ model and its applica­
bility in real-world intrusion detection systems:
 	
– Adaptive Learning for Evolving Threats: 
Implementing continuous learning mechanisms, 
such as reinforcement learning and online training, 
to enable the IDS to adapt dynamically to new and 
evolving attack patterns.
 	
– Privacy-Preserving Techniques: Integrating federated 
learning and homomorphic encryption to enhance 
data security while ensuring effective intrusion 
detection in distributed IoT environments.
 	
– Hybrid Detection Approaches: Combining 
traditional machine learning techniques with deep 
learning-based IDS to improve interpretability, 
reduce false positives, and enhance robustness.
 	
– Optimization for Low-Power Devices: Further 
refining energy-efficient model compression 
techniques, such as pruning, low-rank factorization,

its generalizability and scalability across different 
industry sectors.
 	
– Integration with Blockchain for Enhanced Security: 
Exploring blockchain-based security frameworks to

By addressing these directions, future research can con­
tribute to the continuous improvement of energy-efficient 
and scalable intrusion detection systems, making them 
more resilient against emerging cybersecurity threats while 
ensuring efficient deployment in real-world scenarios.

Abstract: The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) and edge computing technologies has expanded the attack surface for cybercriminals, emphasizing the need for robust and efficient cybersecurity measures. Intrusion detection systems (IDS) are essential defenses; however, deploying traditional IDS solutions on edge devices remains challenging due to limited computational, memory, and energy resources. This research proposes an energy- efficient IDS framework based on a modified Deep Neural Network with Knowledge Distillation and Quantization (DNN-KDQ) to address these challenges. The CICIDS2017 dataset was preprocessed to extract energy-centric features, and adaptive sampling and model compression techniques were applied to optimize performance. The proposed DNN-KDQ model achieves a prediction test accuracy of 99.43%, reduces model size from 196.77 KB to 20.18 KB, and achieves an inference time of 0.07 ms per sample in real-time scenarios. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying high-accuracy, low-latency IDS models on resource-constrained edge devices, contributing to more scalable and energy-efficient cybersecurity solutions for modern network infrastructures.
